title: Sierra Ridge Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Sierra Ridge wells have a 354-foot median depth. See local yields, water levels, permit history, risks and drilling costs.
h1: Sierra Ridge, Colorado Well Depth, Yield and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Sierra Ridge means looking beyond whether a well is already permitted. Records within five miles show how deep local wells tend to be, what reported yields look like, and how much drilling can add to a building budget. The area is in Colorado’s Denver Basin, with permits also naming Lower Dawson, Denver and unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers.

The data is useful for setting expectations, not guaranteeing a result on one lot. A driller still needs to evaluate the parcel, access, geology, casing and grout requirements, pump design, and the water rights tied to the permit.

sections.heading: Sierra Ridge well depth and the Denver Basin geology
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Sierra Ridge is 354 feet. The middle half runs from 205 to 525 feet, so a bid based only on a shallow neighboring well can be misleading. The deepest recorded well is 2,681 feet, while 44% of wells fall between 300 and 600 feet.

Another 16% are 600 feet or deeper, and 18% are under 100 feet. Those figures reflect substantial local variation. The drilling model treats the ground as Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, but permits also identify unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers. Fractured rock can produce uneven results over short distances. Ask for a written price structure that explains the per-foot rate, casing, grout, completion and any added footage.

sections.heading: What Sierra Ridge wells make
sections.html:
Among wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 14.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 11.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Reported yields are concentrated in the useful middle range: 59% produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 41% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

No wells in this record set are reported under 5 gallons per minute. That is encouraging for a buyer, but it is not a promise for an unbuilt well or a particular subdivision lot. A pump test, permit conditions and storage design still matter. Domestic and household wells make up 59% of the use mix, so many records are relevant to residential planning. An exempt household-use well is generally subject to Colorado’s 35-gpm pumping limit.

sections.heading: Water levels near Sierra Ridge: useful history, not a guarantee
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 257 feet, with the middle half between 100 and 430 feet below the surface. That is separate from total well depth: a 354-foot well does not mean water stands at 354 feet.

The decade series does not show a simple continuing decline. Median depth to water was 123 feet in the 1970s, 241 feet in the 1980s, 445 feet in the 2000s, 368 feet in the 2010s and 200 feet in the 2020s. Only 206 records report a static water level, so the measurements are limited and may represent different aquifers, locations and conditions. Use them as background, then request a current well test and water-level measurement.

sections.heading: Sierra Ridge permit history and local drillers
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records contain 5,358 permitted wells within the study area, with 2,686 recorded as constructed. Permits were most numerous in the 1980s with 1,030, followed by the 1970s with 980. The record includes 259 permits from the 2020s, and the newest permit year is 2025.

The most active driller names in these records are Hier Drilling Co Inc (Hier, Bruce A.), with 847 records, and Hier Drilling Co. (Hier, Peter J), with 575. “Authorized (Pe, Pg)” appears on 419 records. These counts describe permit records, not a recommendation or proof of current availability. Verify licensing, insurance, scheduling and the exact scope of any proposal before hiring.

sections.heading: Sierra Ridge well drilling cost at the median depth
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the median depth of 354 feet, the drilled hole comes to about $17,700 to $24,800. A finished well including the pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $23,700 to $36,800.

That range is a budgeting tool, not a fixed quote. Ground conditions, access, casing and grout, water-quality work, electrical distance, pump size and extra drilling can change the final price. Ask each contractor to separate drilling from completion and identify what happens if the hole does not produce enough water. For a rural build near Meridian Village, Stonegate, Stepping Stone or Grand View Estates, compare the well estimate with the full site-development and utility budget.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying a Sierra Ridge lot
sections.html:
Low-yield risk appears limited in the reported data, but a dry hole or poor result is still possible on an individual parcel. Fractured-bedrock conditions can be unpredictable, and a nearby well is not automatically a reliable predictor. Have the seller provide the DWR permit, well construction report, pump test, water-quality results and any maintenance records.

Environmental screening also deserves attention. The mapped area within about ten miles contains 102 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 9 historic mine features and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Their presence does not prove contamination at the property. Test the well water before closing and consider the parcel’s location relative to those sites. Confirm septic setbacks, suitable soil, building area, driveway access and the legal water use allowed by the permit. In an over-appropriated basin, a new well may require an augmentation plan.

sections.heading: A practical plan for building near Sierra Ridge
sections.html:
Start with the well file, not the listing description. Check the permit number, permitted use, aquifer designation, construction report, static level and pump test. Compare neighboring wells around Sierra Ridge, Meridian, Parker and Stonegate, but treat those records as context rather than a guarantee for your lot.

For a new well, obtain a site-specific drilling proposal with a per-foot rate, completion assumptions and a dry-hole or insufficient-yield policy. Budget the modeled finished-well range separately from septic, grading, trenching and electrical work. Before designing the house, confirm that the well’s legal use matches the planned occupancy and that septic and well locations can meet required separation. If the property is in a water-short or over-appropriated area, have the water-rights position reviewed before closing.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Sierra Ridge, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Sierra Ridge is 354 feet. The middle half runs from 205 to 525 feet, while 44% are between 300 and 600 feet. Depth varies by parcel and aquifer, so neighboring permits help with planning but cannot replace a site-specific drilling estimate.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Sierra Ridge?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 354-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $17,700 to $24,800. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $23,700 to $36,800. Access, casing, grout, extra footage and completion choices can change the quote.

faq.q: How much water do Sierra Ridge wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 14.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 11.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. In this record set, 59% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 41% report more than 15. A pump test is still needed to evaluate a specific well.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Sierra Ridge?
faq.a: The records alone cannot establish that a particular well is safe to drink. Within about ten miles, mapped records include 102 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 9 historic mine features and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property’s water before closing and use the results to choose appropriate treatment or follow-up testing.

faq.q: Are Sierra Ridge water levels getting lower?
faq.a: The available decade data does not show a simple continuing decline. Median depth to water was 123 feet in the 1970s, 445 feet in the 2000s and 200 feet in the 2020s. Only 206 wells report static water levels, and measurements may involve different aquifers and conditions, so the series is background rather than a prediction.
